Computer Networking

What is computer network? For example, how does one able to see this webpage? In essense, computer network is the art of communication, despite maybe very far away from each other. More than often, we also have expectations on the network. For example, we want the message is guaranteed to be delivered, or the message is delivered fast enough, say 100s of milliseconds, or the message sent is secure and no one can temper or forge messages. Our ultimate question is: how does the modern network able to achieve all these fancy stuff?

To answer this question, we must be clear about architecture of the computer network, which the rest will be built upon. In the first part, we shall introduce the basic structure of the internet. For the second part, we will dig deep into the protocol stack of the internet in a top-down approach. Finally, in the third part we shall introduce some more applications built upon the fundamentals.

Computer Networks and the Internet

What is the Internet?

Although coined computer network, nowadays it is not just computers: We have mobile phones, laptops, game consoles, or even smart refrigerators - Everything can be linked to the internet! Therefore, we call these network-capable devices as host or end system, both carry the same meaning. In the modern internet, end systems are connected together via communication links and packet switches.

Communication links can be of different physical media, such as coaxial cable, copper wire, optical fibre or radio spectrum, which each has slightly different physical properties (of course). Messages are usually segmented into small packets with additional header bytes at the source, sent via the communication links, and is then reassembles at the destination.

Packet switches receive and forward packets to elsewhere. The most prominent types are routers and link-layer switches. Routers are more used in network cores (deep inside the network), while link-layer switches are more used in access networks (connect end system to the internet).

How does an user becomes part of the internet? We have the Internet Service Providers (ISPs), including local cable or telephone companies, or ISPs for WiFi accesses in public spaces, which provides network access to end systems. Of course, ISPs need to be inter-connected, so lower-tier ISPs are connected to national or international ISPs, forming a hierachical structure.

Finally, protocols are introduced to transfer information on the internet. Since messages are ultimately bitstrings of 0s and 1s, how can we ensure different machines "speak the same language", that is, communicate using the same format? Therefore, internet standards are developed by the Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF), where the IETF release documents as requests for comments (RFCs). Some of the well-known protocols are defined in the RFCs, such as the Transmission Control Protocol (TCP) [RFC 793], Internet Protocol (IP) [RFC 791] and Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP) [RFC 2616].

We may consider the internet as an infrastructure that provides services to various distributed applications, such as web surfing, peer-to-peer (P2P) file sharing, remote login, and many more. It would be stupid if we need to reinvent how to send message to each other for every distributed application we made! Therefore, the end systems of the internet provides Application Programming Interface (API) for delivering data, which we can rely on this encapsulation to develop new applications easily.

The Network Edge

Applications and end systems run at the "edge of the network" (in the spherical sense). What forms the access network, which physically connects the end system to the first (edge) router? We split into three types of access networks - home, enterprise and wide-area mobile wireless.

Access in Home

There are telephone and cable televison companies out there, both are going to be killed by the internet. How can they make more money? As the saying goes, "if you can't beat them, join them", of course by becoming Internet Service Providers (ISPs)! They are the two most prominent home access solutions these days.

First, we have the digital subscriber line (DSL) provided by the local telephone company (telco). Since the ordinary telephone channel only uses 0 to 4 kHz band of the phone line to transmit human voice, it can carry data from 4 kHz to 1 MHz band at the same time. A DSL modem (Modulator-Demodulator, digital to analogue and analogue to digital) is used to convert digital data to analogue high-frequency signals, which is then converted back to digital signals at the Digital Subscriber Line Access Multiplexer (DSLAM) at the central office (CO) of the telco. With DSL, we can reach 24 Mbps downstream and 2.5 Mbps upstream (in 2003). An older technique is dial-up, where we use the ordinary telephone channel to access the internet. Its speed is capped by 56 Kbps, and we cannot call with traditional telephone and access internet at the same time.

How about cables? Similar to DSL, we can reuse the infrastructure of the (analogue) cable television. Fibre (optic) cables is used for fast transmittion to neighbourhood-level junction (for 500 ~ 5000 homes), then coaxial (copper) cables is used to connected to each home. Therefore, it is also referred as hybrid fibre coax (HFC). We need a cable modem to convert between digital and analogue, which is connected to the computer via an Ethernet port. This is somewhat faster than DSL, and can reach 42.8 Mbps downstream and 30.7 Mbps upstream. Note that by the nature of cable television, the bandwidth is shared among the homes! Therefore, a newer technology is the fibre to the home (FTTH), directly connecting the optic fibre to the home, which can achieve an even higher speed.

As a final remark, satellite links can be used as well, such as Starlink.

Access in Enterprise

Local area networks (LAN) can be used to connect end systems to their edge router (access point). Why do we need LAN when we have DSL and cable already? Let's consider an example: Let's say there is a computer laboratory with 100 computers - It make no sense to have 100 cables from the laboratory to the ISP! Therefore, what we will do is to aggregate the traffic via the LAN, then connect to the edge router. There are two kinds of prevalent access technologies - The Ethernet and the WiFi.

For Ethernet, the hosts are connected to the Ethernet switch by physical wires (coaxial / twisted-pair / fibre optics), where nowadays the access speed can be up to several Gbps. On the other hand, WiFi, or more formally wireless LAN access or IEEE 802.11, offers a wireless access point for mobile devices within few tens of metres.

Wide-area Mobile Wireless Access

In the modern days, we also have 3G / 4G / 5G (Generation) networks, which can reach up to several kilometres of radius. You may ask: What is the main difference between this and WiFi? The signals are transmitted in a licensed portion of the spectrum, and so it may carry a high-power and so pass a large distance. This is not the case for WiFi.

The Network Core

Alright, now you have access to the Internet. How shall the message be transferred between you and others? We can take inspiration from postal services and traditional telephones. For postal services, we do not care about what stations the mail has passed through, as long as the mail can arrive at its destination; while for traditional telephones, the pathway is created at the beginning of the telephone call. These two ways of switching are called the packet-switched and circuit-switched respectively.

Packet-Switching

The modern Internet uses packets. Most packet switches use the Store-and-Forward Transmission, which only starts forwarding after it receives the entire packet. For each of the outgoing link, we have an output buffer to store the packets to be sent. If many packets arrive in a shortburst, the packets would have to wait, and so this induces queueing delays; or even if the buffer is completely full, then packet loss would occur, which packets would be dropped and lost forever. The packet switches use forwarding tables to decide which outgoing link to forward the packet to, and routing protocols are used to set forwarding tables automatically to route the packets.

Circuit-Switching

For circuit-switching, the bandwidth (transmittion rate) on each of the used communication link is reserved for the end-to-end connection, which the connection is referred as a circuit. Like traditional telephone, we can expect to have a guaranteed constant rate throughout the connection, which cannot be achieved by packet-switching. A question is: how can we allocate a communication link for multiple circuits? We can do this via the means of multiplexing. In frequency-division multiplexing (FDM), we subdivide the band into smaller frequency bands, and for time-division multiplexing (TDM) we segment the time domain into periodic time slots.

The reason why the current day Internet prefers packet-switching rather than circuit-switching is simple: We do not want to waste idle resources. Let's say you are using the Internet where you only download rarely (say 10% of the time), then the other 90% of time the bandwidth will go to waste for circuit-switching! The efficiency of packet-switching is simply much better in terms of the bandwidth usage.

Network Hierachy

Now, we will briefly mention the hierachy of networks - namely how the ISPs (and others) are inter-connected together. In fact, this is more of a social construct and driven by economy. Imagine there is only one global transit ISP, and each access ISP connects to it. The access ISP is the customer and the global ISP is the provider, which the access ISP pays to keep its service up. Naturally, companies want to build their own global transit ISPs to earn money. In practice, the global transit ISPs are called tier-1 ISPs, while there are also regional ISPs which connects ISPs in a region.

There are many more things in the network of network. The Point of Presenses (PoP) is a group of routers where the customer ISPs can connect to the provider ISP; A customer ISP can multi-home and connect to multiple provider ISPs; Nearby ISPs at the same level can peer by connecting their network together; while Internet Exchange Points (IXP) are set up for multiple ISPs to peer together. Finally, we have content provider networks, which large companies such as Google attempts to bypass the fee for traffic through tier-1 ISPs by setting a network on its own, and peering IXPs and lower-tier ISPs.

Delay, Loss and Throughput for Packets

Let us turn our focus back to packet-switched networks. How can we rate whether a network is good or bad? The most common metrics are packet delay (time taken from begin send to done receive), packet loss (percentage of packets never reaching destination) and throughput (number of bytes or packets sent through the network per second).

We can split packet delays into four types of delays naturally - just imagine a packet arrives at a switch. The packet header is examined to check its destination, while checksums are computed to check whether the packet is corrupted. All these computations induces (nodal) processing delay. After being processed, the packet enters the output buffer of the switch. It has to wait for its turn, incurring queueing delay. When it is the packet's turn to be sent, the packet is sent at a certain transmittion speed, costing transmittion delay. Finally, it takes time for the information to propagate through the physical media, say copper wire, fibre optics or air, leading to propagation delay. We can express the total nodal delay as dnodal = dproc + dqueue + dtrans + dprop.

It might not be apparent for the difference between transmittion delay and propagation delay. Transmittion delay depends on the switch, which relates to the speed for the switch to generate signal. On the other hand, propagation delay depends on the physical media of the link, which relates to the traverse speed of the information as light, wave or whatever fancy stuff.

Note that processing delay, queueing delay and propagation delay are all constants with the exception of queueing delay. How shall we estimate the average queueing delay at a switch? Denote the traffic intensity ρ as the ratio between incoming byte rate (La) and transmission rate (R). Clearly if ρ is greater than 1, then the queue will grow indefinitely and the queueing delay tends to infinity (of course, the packet will be dropped in reality, since the output buffer is finite). Hence, we assume ρ is at most 1. Considering this as a random process, by little's formula we have dqueue = ρdnodal. Therefore, ignoring processing delay, we have dqueue = dtrans ρ / (1 - ρ), and the average queueing delay approaches infinity as ρ approaches 1.

Finally, we briefly mention the throughput of a packet-switched network. Consider the over-simplified case where there are N communication links between the server and the client connected in a chain, then the transmittion speed is limited by the slowest link, the bottleneck link.

Protocol Layers and Their Service Models

The network is a complicated matter, and is continuously evolving. Back then, dial-up might be sufficient, but now we more use WiFi or Ethernet. Obviously, we want our distribution application to be independent of the nature of the communication link, and it should equally work if we use OCR on paper carried by pigeons! We want to split the resposibility of the network into multiple parts, so that the protocols within the same layer or with the same functionality can be switched when there are newer and faster inventions.

Here comes the protcol layers or protocol stack: Each layer offers some promises on their services which their upper layers is built upon. In the Internet Prtocol Stack, from top to down we have Application Layer (communication between applications), Transport Layer (end-to-end transport between processes), Network Layer (transfer data between hosts), Link Layer (transfer data across communication links) and Physical Layer (transfer bits via physical media).

Conventionally, we call packets in different layers with distinct names to be more specific: we would say application message, transport segment, network datagram and link frame. The International Organisation for Standardisation (ISO) proposes a seven-layer Open Systems Interconnection (OSI) model with the addition of Presentation Layer and Session Layer between Application Layer and Transport Layer, although these are less important compare to the other five. Each lower layer encapsulates the packets it receive from the upper layer by prepanding header bytes, which acts as the control bytes for that layer, and is removed when the data is passed up again.

Networks Under Attack

The network is a delicate matter. If done wrong, it can be attacked as easily as talk to a person in real life. Here, we wish to briefly classify different types of network attacks. First, the Internet contains malwares which can infect our devices, which may delete files, install spyware or mine bitcoins. These malwares are often self-replicating, which it can replicate themselves and attempt to infect other hosts. We say a malware is virus when it requires some form of user interaction, and worm otherwise. These network attacks can also be targeting servers for denial-of-service (DoS) attacks. Payloads maybe crafted to trigger vulnerabilities, or attempt to flood the bandwidth of the access link or TCP connection pool of the server. The more common form of DoS is DDoS, meaning it is distributed, since it is easier to generate huge amount of traffic that way.

Other than active attacks, hackers can also sniff packets when other users connecting to WiFi or Ethernet whenever packets are broadcasted or the hacker gained access to the access router. When the packets themselves are unencrypted, then the hacker can peek at the message you receive or sent. On the other hand, hackers can also do IP spoofing, pretending to be other hosts by faking the source IP address and sent malicious commands. Hence, end-point authentication can be used to check the origins of the messages.

Application Layer

Principles of Network Applications

What are network applications? Simply speaking, those are programs that is distributed onto different end systems, which communicate using the Internet. These applications usually adopts either the client-server architecture or the peer-to-peer (P2P) architecture, which decides whom the end systems should be communicating with.

Application Architecture

For the client-server architecture, the application provider uses a dedicated server (or a group of servers) to respond to the requests of the users. We usually refer to who makes requests as client and whoever responds as server. Meanwhile, for a P2P architecture, the content is sent from anyone to anyone. We can see that a benefit of P2P is its self-scalability: if many people joins, then its upload bandwidth also increases proportionally.

Sockets and Ports

From the point of view of the application, the network transport services provides a logical end-to-end transport between processes on different hosts. How does a running program, a process, use the transport services provided by the operating system? The kernel allows processes to create socket, an interface between the process and the kernel, which can then be used to send and receive data across the Internet. The process can only specify a small set of parameters to the transport layer, but not interfere with the network functionality of the hardware directly.

Since multiple processes can be running on the same host, ports are introduced for identification of the processes. The ports are identified with a 16-bit number, which 0 ~ 1023 are reserved ports (requires sudo perm on unix) for well-known applications (21: FTP, 25: SMTP, 53: DNS, 80: HTTP, 443: HTTPS), while 1024 ~ 65535 are ephemeral (temporary) ports. A way of thinking is that the usage of ports is a way to multiplexing upon network layer, since the network layer by design only deals with sending packets between hosts.

Transport Services

Suppose there are several transport-layer protocols to choose from. Which should you pick for the application? Of course, we shall consider the services that these protocols have promised. Perhaps the most important thing is reliable data transfer (rdt) (opposite: loss-tolerant), which both hosts are assured that the packet has been sent. We also care about the bandwidth when the application is bandwidth-sensitive (opposite: elastic), for instance real-time gaming or trading. There are also other promises on timing or security.

In reality, the applications always use either the Transmittion Control Protocol (TCP) or the User Datagram Protocol (UDP). TCP offers reliable data transfer and congestion control, while UDP offers nothing(!) Note that there is no any guarantees on timing or bandwidth - the Internet only do its best effort. One may ask - if UDP offers nothing, why do we use UDP? The reason is that since UDP is simpler, it provides more control to the application layer, which is sometimes needed when you need ultra-low latency or you expect it to work even under congestion. The Secure Sockets Layer (SSL) is an extension upon TCP, which an extra layer of encryption / decryption is done before and after sending packets via TCP.

Application Protocols

The application protocol specifies the syntax and the semantics of the messages. The current Internet is built upon many simple but elegant protocols, such as HyperText Transfer Protocol (HTTP) for website, File Transfer Protocol (FTP) for file transfer, Simple Mail Transfer Protocol (SMTP) for electronic mail transfer, Post-Office Protocol - Version 3 (POP3) or Internet Mail Access Protocol (IMAP) for electronic mail access, Domain Name System (DNS) for resolving domain name, and many more.

Interestingly, all of them uses TCP, except that the DNS uses UDP. The reason why we use UDP for DNS is that if the network is congested, you cannot use the Internet anyways, and it is better not to congest it even more. We will go through these well-known application protocols one-by-one, and most importantly, gain some insights over their protocol designs.
